conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here today to get your third dose of high-dose methotrexate for your lymphoma. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay. A bit tired and weak, but that’s been going on. My mouth is still sore from the last round, but it’s getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the mucositis can take time to heal. We’ll keep managing that with mouth rinses and pain meds. You’re scheduled for the methotrexate infusion tomorrow. Today, we’ll run some labs and give you IVIG for your immune deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I had that last time, right? The IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every three weeks. We’ll give you 40 grams today with Tylenol and Benadryl first to prevent reactions. Any allergies we should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to penicillin, sulfa, morphine, omeprazole, and a few others. They’re all listed, I think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we see that. We’ll avoid those. Your breathing and heart sounds look good on the chest X-ray. No fluid in the lungs. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I haven’t had any shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your kidney function closely during chemo. Methotrexate can affect the kidneys, so we’ll give you lots of fluids and check labs frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My sugars have been high lately. I know you’re watching that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar was 219 today. At home you’re on metformin, and you say it’s under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, between 80 and 160. But I eat better at home. Here, I’ve had some snacks—maybe too many crackers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain the higher readings. We may need insulin while you're here, but we’ll be cautious about low sugars, especially with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll try to stick to the diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your methotrexate infusion. Dose is 3.5 grams per square meter. You’re tolerating it well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor for nausea, mouth sores, and kidney issues. You’ll get leucovorin later to help clear the drug. We expect you to clear it within 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your methotrexate levels are dropping well—0.31 yesterday, now 0.04. That means your body is clearing the drug as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. It means lower risk of toxicity. Your weakness from the brain lymphoma is also improving, which is a positive sign the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger than I did after the fall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned more abdominal pain and gas today. Given your history of bowel perforation, we did a KUB. No obstruction or free air—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s crampy and I’m passing a lot of gas. My ostomy output is higher too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on clear liquids for now and send a stool test to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first stool test came back negative for C. diff. But since symptoms continue, we’re repeating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurts. I hope it’s not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray shows no obstruction. But we’re concerned enough to do a CT scan today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with contrast. It will help us see if there’s inflammation or infection in the bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. There’s wall thickening in your small bowel and some air outside the intestine. It’s likely infection or inflammation, not ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? From what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat stool test just came in positive for C. difficile. That’s likely the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your medical history. But we’re starting oral vancomycin right away—125 mg four times a day for 14 days. That should clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will that affect my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked—no major interactions. We’ll keep monitoring your kidney and liver labs too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain is improving, and your ostomy output is coming down. That’s a good sign the vancomycin is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Still bloated, but less pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on vancomycin for the full course. Also, your blood sugar has been high—up to 497. We started Lantus insulin and adjusted your sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I ate those extra crackers. Won’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. But at home, if sugars stay high, you might need insulin long-term. We ordered an A1C, but it’s pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch my diet more carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is low—2.0. We’re giving one dose of Neupogen to help boost it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s standard after chemo. It helps your body make white blood cells faster and lowers infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I give it myself at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you have the supplies. We’ll send one dose home with instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my dexamethasone? I’ve been on 2 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re tapering it down to 1 mg twice a day. Since your brain swelling is better, we can reduce it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects from lowering it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel tired or achy during taper, but we’ll monitor. It’s important to avoid sudden stops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is gone, C. diff treatment is on track, and your lymphoma treatment was successful. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, plus oral vancomycin for 12 more days. Dexamethasone is now 1 mg twice a day. And you’ll take Neupogen tonight if you have it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow-up appointment on ___ at 2:30 PM. You’ll also return for your next chemo admission on ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll mark it down. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the clear diet until the vancomycin is done. Watch for fever, worsening pain, or diarrhea. Call us if any of those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my mouth sores. Any new advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using the magic mouthwash. They should continue improving. Hydration and soft foods help too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking a lot of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That helps with both mucositis and kidney clearance of meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ostomy? It’s still active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s settling. As the infection clears, output should normalize. Keep the skin clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have supplies at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And remember, no NSAIDs—they can irritate your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I only take my prescribed pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing everything right. We’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The nurse will go over your discharge papers now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your CMV test came back negative. No active infection there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your immune system is challenged, so we check regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll let the team know you’re ready for discharge prep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest and take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you at your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Ms. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the oncology team. We're admitting you today for your fourth cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your lymphoma. How have you been feeling since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been more tired than usual and passing a lot of gas. My ostomy output has slowed down a bit, but it’s still more than normal. No fevers or nausea, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We know you were on vancomycin for C. diff from your last admission. Are you still taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking it every six hours like they told me. It helped, but I still have some gas and foamy stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll keep you on the vancomycin during this stay. We’ll also check a stool sample to make sure the C. diff is fully cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried if it’s still positive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Sometimes the test can stay positive even after the infection is gone. We’ll focus on your symptoms and whether your output improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My back pain is also acting up—same as always. I’ve been using my usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your methadone, oxycodone, and cyclobenzaprine. Pain control is important, especially during chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m also a bit nervous about the methotrexate—last time I had bad mouth sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re using a lower dose again—3500 mg/m² instead of 8000. We’ll also start leucovorin 24 hours after the infusion to help protect your cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fluids with baking soda? I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll give you IV fluids with sodium bicarbonate to keep your urine alkaline. That helps your kidneys clear the methotrexate safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my blood sugar? It’s been high at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it closely. We’ve held your metformin for now and will use insulin to keep your sugars in check. You need good nutrition, so we don’t want to restrict your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’ve been trying to eat more, but it’s hard with the fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you with IV fluids and nutrition as needed. Let’s get you settled, and I’ll come back after the chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray looks clear—no fluid or infection. That’s great. We’re cleared to start the methotrexate infusion tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Any other tests today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drew blood for labs, including your kidney and liver function. Your potassium is a bit low, so we’ll start replacing it with IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been losing a lot through the ostomy. Should I take supplements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start oral potassium and magnesium. You’ll go home with those too, to help keep your levels stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re about to start your methotrexate infusion. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just the usual back pain. I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll begin now. The infusion will take a few hours. We’ll monitor your urine pH and keep you well-hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You did well. We’ll start checking your methotrexate levels tomorrow and the day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My mouth already feels a little dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start using Caphasol and Gelclair to keep your mouth moist and prevent sores. We also noticed some white patches—could be early thrush.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not serious, but we want to treat it. We’re starting fluconazole to clear it up and prevent it from coming back during your low counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test came back negative for C. diff toxin. That’s good news—means the infection is likely resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can stop the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on it for now. Your output is still high, and with your short gut, we want to be cautious. We’re also starting a short course of rifaximin to help with bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first methotrexate level is 0.54, which is expected. It’s coming down appropriately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Started last night, and we’ll continue it until your levels are undetectable. It helps protect your healthy cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth feels sore. The patches are spreading a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s mild mucositis, common with methotrexate. Keep using the Caphasol and Gelclair. The fluconazole will help with the fungal component.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your second methotrexate level is 0.02—great. It’s clearing well. Your kidney function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still running high—mostly in the 200s and 300s. We’re keeping you on insulin. We’ll transition back to metformin at home, but we need to control it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to eat better when I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know it’s tough. Your nutrition is more important right now than perfect sugar control. We’ll support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last methotrexate level is <0.02—undetectable. That means you’ve cleared the drug safely. Great job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My mouth is feeling better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fluconazole and mouth care are working. We’ll send it home with you as a preventive measure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your labs are stable, and you’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the vancomycin and supplements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue vancomycin at home as directed by your outpatient team. We’re sending potassium and magnesium supplements with refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fluconazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one tablet daily to prevent fungal infections when your counts are low. We’re also adding acyclovir for viral protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need IVIG for your immune deficiency and pentamidine for PCP prophylaxis. Your oncology team will coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ve reviewed everything, and you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any final instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all new medications as prescribed. Monitor your blood sugar, stay hydrated, and call if you develop fever, worsening mouth sores, or abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—I take the potassium once a day and magnesium twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. And the fluconazole and acyclovir daily. Your pharmacy will have all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your discharge papers and prescriptions ready shortly. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse said my ostomy bag needs changing every few days. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep an eye on the skin around it. If it gets red or sore, use the barrier cream we sent home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take it easy and follow up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—when should I restart my regular pain meds routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already on them—methadone, oxycodone, and cyclobenzaprine. Just follow the discharge instructions and call if pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be helping manage your care during this admission. You're here for your fifth cycle of high-dose methotrexate for the lymphoma in your colon and brain, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’m ready to get started. I hope this one goes better than the first—those mouth sores were awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you had mucositis before, so we’ve reduced the dose again to 3500 mg/m² to help prevent that. We’ll also start leucovorin 24 hours after the infusion to protect your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes me feel better. I’ve been managing my diabetes with metformin at home—should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold the metformin while you’re here because of the IV fluids and kidney monitoring. We’ll check your glucose regularly and use insulin if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I’ve been on insulin before during past stays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also need to check a chest X-ray before starting chemo to make sure there’s no fluid or infection. It was done earlier—looks clear, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that vancomycin for C. diff since last time. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued it with approval from infectious disease. You’ll keep taking it at home until your doctor advises stopping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. My back pain’s been stable—I’m still on methadone and oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your pain regimen the same. Just let us know if it’s not controlled. Also, we noticed the skin on your tailbone is broken down. The wound team will come by to assess it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been like that since the first chemo cycle. It’s hard to sit for long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll recommend a special dressing and ways to relieve pressure. We’ll also moisturize your elbows—they looked a bit red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. When will the chemo start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s already been ordered. We’ll start the infusion in about an hour. We’ll give you fluids with sodium bicarbonate to keep your urine alkaline—that helps the methotrexate clear safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. How often will you check my levels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your methotrexate blood levels every 24 hours. Once they drop to undetectable levels on two consecutive days, you can go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the IVIG? I’m due for that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get your IV immunoglobulin on day three—Wednesday. We’ll premedicate you to prevent reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I also take acyclovir for herpes—still need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue it. You’ll also get inhaled pentamidine today to prevent a type of pneumonia, since your immune system is suppressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It’s the one I inhale after using the albuterol, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re very familiar with your care—that helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your first methotrexate level came back this morning. It’s where we expect it to be. You’re doing well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any issues with my blood work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is low—2.5—and your platelets are 100. We’ll watch closely. No fever yet, so no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s expected. We’ll keep you on neutropenic precautions—no fresh flowers or raw fruit, and we’ll screen visitors for illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll stick to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you your IVIG this morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little headache, but not bad. I took some acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your urine culture came back—no significant bacteria, so no UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Any update on my methotrexate levels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re coming down as expected. Your last level was low, and today’s should be even lower. We’re on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your methotrexate level is now undetectable. That’s excellent. We’ll repeat it tomorrow to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We also need your absolute neutrophil count to recover a bit. It’s still low, so we’ll keep you for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t mind staying if it’s safer. I just don’t want to risk infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re being cautious. Your diabetes has been stable on the sliding scale—glucose mostly under 180.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll go back to metformin at home, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart it at discharge. And you’ll continue vancomycin at home for the C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your methotrexate level is undetectable for the second day, and your ANC is now 1030. You’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with a week’s supply of methadone and oxycodone. Your PCP manages your contract, so follow up with them soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And the wound care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For your tailbone, use Duoderm gel and cover with Mepilex—change every three days. For your elbows, apply Aloe Vesta and protect with a bandage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other meds changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re simplifying dexamethasone to 1 mg daily and reducing dronabinol. Everything else stays the same, including acyclovir and pentamidine monthly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review the list with my pharmacist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oncology team wants to see you in two days. Call them if you develop fever, chills, or any sores in your mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you this morning. The nurse will go over your meds and wound care one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. It’s good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the chemo well—no mucositis, which is a big win. Just keep monitoring your counts and blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll check my glucose twice a day like always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And remember—no NSAIDs because of your colostomy and kidney concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to acetaminophen. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge paperwork now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this admission. You’re here for your next dose of high-dose methotrexate for your lymphoma. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay, a bit tired, but no major pain. I’m just hoping this round goes better than the last one—I had really bad mouth sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That was from the higher dose. This time we’re using 3500 mg/m², which is lower and should be easier on you. We’ll also start leucovorin rescue 24 hours after the infusion to help protect your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Will I need blood tests during this stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll check your methotrexate levels daily to make sure they’re going down properly. We also need to monitor your kidneys and blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my diabetes—should I keep taking metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold metformin while you’re here because of the chemotherapy. Your sugars will be checked regularly, and you can restart it when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my ostomy—lately I’ve had more output and some belly pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested a stool sample, and it came back positive for C. diff. That’s likely causing the symptoms. We’ve started you on oral vancomycin to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I had that before. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your immune system being low, but we caught it early. The treatment should clear it up in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m also on pentamidine monthly—is that happening this stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s scheduled for tomorrow. It’s to prevent lung infections due to your immune deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Last time I had some trouble breathing after it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. If you have any wheezing, we can give albuterol right away. We’ll also give pre-medications to reduce the risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, that makes me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to start your methotrexate infusion. It’ll take a few hours. A nurse will be with you the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Any side effects I should watch for now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nausea or headache are possible. Let us know right away if you feel short of breath, dizzy, or have a rash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a bit nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you some ondansetron to help with that. Drink small sips of water if you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level is 0.50, which is where we expect it. Your kidneys are handling it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel okay—just a little tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give your IVIG today to support your immune system. It’s part of your regular treatment for common variable immune deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, every three weeks. Does it help prevent infections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it gives your body the antibodies it can’t make on its own. It’s important with your lymphoma and chemotherapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: After the pentamidine, I started wheezing a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you an albuterol nebulizer, and your breathing improved. No oxygen was needed. It’s a known reaction, but we’ll watch you closely next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m glad it passed quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your methotrexate level is now 0.04, and it should drop to undetectable by tomorrow. That means the leucovorin is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow, if everything stays on track. We’ll check one more level to confirm it’s cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain—it’s been flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can adjust your methadone or add cyclobenzaprine if needed. Let’s try an extra dose now and see how you feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain’s better now, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also stopped your levofloxacin. It’s no longer needed, and we want to avoid unnecessary antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the vancomycin for C. diff—how long will I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish a 10-day course at home. We’ll send it with you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest methotrexate level is undetectable. That’s excellent. We can plan for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take leucovorin for one more day—two tablets every six hours for five doses. Continue the vancomycin, and restart metformin as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—everything else stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, except we’re changing your dronabinol dose to 2.5 mg twice a day. It should help with nausea and appetite without making you too drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch how I feel on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled your next methotrexate cycle in a few weeks. Your oncologist will confirm the date.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my IVIG—same schedule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three weeks from your last dose. Your infusion center will contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a couple of hours. A nurse will review your medications and home instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’m glad this round went smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep monitoring your ostomy and call if you have fever, severe pain, or breathing trouble. Otherwise, see you at your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I watch for mouth sores this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lower dose makes that less likely. But if you notice any sores, start using the magic mouthwash and let your team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my thyroid—do I need a blood test soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your levothyroxine dose is stable. Your primary doctor can check your levels at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’ll take potassium supplements too—four capsules daily with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that for my heart or muscles?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both. Chemo and C. diff can lower potassium. This helps keep your levels safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll take it with dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your ostomy care again before you leave. Any final questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m all set. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you for your next treatment. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, just to confirm—I take the leucovorin every six hours starting today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, two tablets every six hours for five total doses. That’s one day’s worth. It helps clear any remaining chemo from your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll set an alarm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be overseeing your care during this admission. You're here for your seventh cycle of high-dose methotrexate for the lymphoma in your brain. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Doctor. I’m feeling okay overall. A bit tired, but no headaches or vision problems. My back pain is the usual, and my ostomy has been more active lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting me know. We saw in your labs that your magnesium is low, which can happen with high ostomy output. We’ll start IV fluids and give you some magnesium to correct that before we begin chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I did try taking more magnesium pills, but it made me nauseous and increased the output. So I cut back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. We’ll manage it more carefully with IVs this time. We also noticed your white blood cell count is low. That’s common with chemo, but we’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that delay the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We want to make sure your counts are stable. We’ll check them again tomorrow. For now, focus on resting and staying hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my diabetes meds—should I keep taking metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold the metformin while you’re here, just like last time. We’ll use insulin if your sugars go up. It’s safer with the chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my thyroid and asthma meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking your levothyroxine daily. For asthma, use your albuterol if you feel tightness. But so far, your breathing sounds clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are back. The magnesium is improving with the IV, but your white count dipped a bit more overnight. We’ll wait one more day before starting chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that going to be a problem? I was hoping to get it done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But giving chemo when your counts are too low increases infection risk. We’ll recheck this afternoon. If it stabilizes, we can proceed tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust your judgment. Any other tests today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent a stool test to check for infections since your ostomy output is high. It came back negative for C. diff, parasites, and viruses. So it’s likely related to your magnesium and chemo history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it was another infection like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re being cautious. We also tested for CMV, which can affect the gut, but that was negative too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Update: your white count has stabilized. It’s still low, but not dropping. We’re comfortable proceeding with chemo tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Will it be the same dose as last few times?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 3.5 grams per square meter. We reduced it after the severe mucositis you had at the higher dose. This one has been much better tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that. I don’t want to go through that again. Will I get the leucovorin after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll start leucovorin 24 hours after the infusion to protect you. We’ll also give IV bicarbonate to help flush the methotrexate out through your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, plenty of IV fluids throughout. We’ll keep you well-hydrated to protect your kidneys and help clear the drug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. We’re going to start the methotrexate infusion in about an hour. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling okay. A little anxious, but ready to get it done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll monitor you closely. The nurse will check your vitals every few hours and we’ll draw blood to track the methotrexate levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You tolerated it very well—no nausea, no drop in blood pressure. Great job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I didn’t feel much at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly what we want. We’ll keep the IV fluids going and start bicarbonate. Tomorrow, we’ll begin leucovorin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your methotrexate level is coming down as expected. We’ve started oral leucovorin—two tablets every six hours for three doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I take that at home too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take three more doses at home. We’ll send six tablets with you—take two every six hours, starting from the first dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds—can I restart metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll wait until your methotrexate level is undetectable. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: your latest methotrexate level is 0.08. Still a bit high, so we’ll keep monitoring. You’re doing well otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s trending down. We expect it to be below 0.05 by tomorrow, which is when we can safely discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. Your methotrexate level is now 0.03—below the threshold. Your kidneys are handling it well, and your counts are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discharge you later this morning. We’ll review your meds and give you instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge plan. You’ll continue leucovorin at home for three doses. Restart metformin as two 500 mg tablets in the morning and two at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s different from before. I was taking 1000 mg at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re adjusting it to reduce GI side effects. Also, start taking magnesium oxide—one tablet twice daily. That should help without worsening ostomy output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue methadone, oxycodone as needed, and we’ve switched pregabalin to bedtime only to help with sleep and nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your oncologist in a week. They’ll review your progress and plan the next steps. Call if you develop fever, mouth sores, or severe diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. You’re alert, walking well, and your vitals are stable. All set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will bring your discharge paperwork and prescriptions. Someone will assist you to the car.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you at your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, you too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.
