conversation_lines.text: We hope so. Duloxetine and pregabalin are now both at bedtime to simplify your schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s easier. I sometimes forget the duloxetine during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your methotrexate level is safe, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What’s the plan for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have labs checked soon. The oncology team will review your MRI results to decide whether the next treatment will be more methotrexate or R-CHOP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope the tumor is shrinking. I’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You really have. You’ve tolerated this well, and that’s a big win. Keep taking your meds, avoid illness, and call if you develop fever or mouth sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take the leucovorin on time and watch for any nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and use ondansetron if needed. You have it prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cipro—I take that with or without food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With food to avoid stomach upset. Twice a day for seven days, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll set reminders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re doing well. Rest, stay hydrated, and take it easy for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my ostomy. Any concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No issues noted. Keep monitoring output and stay hydrated. Call if you see major changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Ms. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I see you're here for your scheduled high-dose methotrexate treatment today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I just got back from vacation and wanted to stay on track with my treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. I noticed in your history you mentioned some stomach discomfort over the last couple of days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh yes, after a barbecue. I ate pineapple and had some cramps. I passed chunks in my ostomy, but no vomiting or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of lymphoma in the colon, we want to be careful. We’ll hold off on methotrexate today and do a CT scan to check your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that serious? Could it be the cancer coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be many things—maybe just irritation from food. But we need to rule out lymphoma recurrence. The CT will help us see what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, that makes sense. I’ve been feeling okay otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan showed some thickening in part of your small intestine. It could be infection or inflammation, but one area looks a bit concerning for possible lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Does that mean the cancer is back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. The appearance could also be from an infection. We’ve started you on antibiotics—ciprofloxacin and metronidazole—just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will we know for sure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled an upper enteroscopy for today. It will let us look directly into your small bowel. Unfortunately, the scope may not reach the farthest area of concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we might not get a full answer from it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. If needed, we can do an MR enterography later, which gives a more detailed view. But for now, the enteroscopy will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The enteroscopy is done. We saw mild gastritis, but the small bowel looked normal. No ulcers or masses where we could see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very encouraging. But remember, the scope didn’t reach the farthest area that looked thick on the CT. So we can’t completely rule out lymphoma there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your symptoms have improved—you’re not having pain or odd ostomy output anymore. That suggests this might have been an infection that’s resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably not cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but less likely. We’ll keep monitoring. You have a PET scan scheduled soon—that will help us see if there’s any active disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about my methotrexate? I was supposed to get it this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We decided to hold it this time. With the GI symptoms and uncertainty, it’s safer to wait. We don’t want to suppress your immune system during a possible infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. When would I get the next dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss it after your PET scan and GI follow-up. Likely in a few weeks, depending on results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your usual meds. We did increase your pantoprazole to twice daily for the gastritis we saw.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for five days total. That’s four more doses after today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes and immune deficiency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is stable. Keep taking metformin. And your IVIG is scheduled every three weeks—you’re due soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about everything piling up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But right now, you’re doing well. No fever, pain is gone, labs are stable. We’re leaning toward this being a mild infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’ve improved, and there’s no sign of ongoing infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop abdominal pain, fever, or changes in ostomy output, let us know. Otherwise, keep taking your antibiotics and follow up with GI next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PET scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, go to that as scheduled. We’ll use those results to decide if you need more imaging or can restart methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing we’re on top of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we checked your stool, and it was negative for C. diff and other infections. That supports our idea of a mild, self-limited issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your oncology and GI teams updated. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot. I’ll make sure to keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You can go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about 10 days ago, but got much worse in the last few days. Yesterday was the worst—had one episode of vomiting food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Does the pain get worse with movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, moving makes it worse. But eating doesn’t seem to affect it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, or weight loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fevers or chills. Weight’s been stable. But my colostomy output has decreased, and the stool is like rabbit pellets. One was whitish.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I also see you mentioned a neighbor had similar symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she had nausea and stomach issues too. Thought maybe it was something going around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possible, but given your history of lymphoma and bowel surgery, we need to be cautious. We’ve ordered a CT scan to check for any blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this be related to my lymphoma coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but we won’t know until we see the scan. The thickening in the bowel could be infection, inflammation, or early lymphoma. We’ll start you on IV fluids and antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’m on so many meds already—will they change anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding metformin while you’re not eating much. Otherwise, we’ll keep your other meds running—like your methadone for pain and Cymbalta for mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT results are back. There’s a segment of small bowel that’s dilated near a past surgical connection. There’s fecalized material and some new wall thickening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a partial functional obstruction—your bowel isn’t moving things through well. The anastomosis is open, so it’s not a complete blockage. We’re calling GI and colorectal surgery to review.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the thickening—could it be lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule it out, but there’s no clear evidence of progression. Your lymph nodes haven’t changed much, and your spleen is only mildly enlarged, as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on antibiotics for now—cefepime and flagyl—just in case it’s infection. But if you stay afebrile and improve, we’ll stop them. No surgery needed at this point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. Pain is much less. Haven’t vomited again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs show your white count dropped a bit, but it’s likely due to your immune condition. Stool tests came back negative—no C. diff, no parasites, no salmonella.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t look like it. We’re going to stop the antibiotics. GI thinks this was a temporary motility issue—maybe a functional obstruction that’s resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the lymphoma concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still can’t rule it out completely, but no signs of active disease. Your head MRI was done yesterday—results pending, but no red flags so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my colostomy—will it go back to normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, output should normalize as your bowel function improves. We’ll advance your diet today—start with clear liquids, then soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on the soft diet—no nausea, pain is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain, and I’ve had a few good meals. Colostomy is more active now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep you overnight for observation. GI wants you to get a magnetic resonance enterography—MRE—after discharge to check bowel function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a CT or MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an MRI focused on the bowel. It gives better detail than CT for soft tissue and motility. You’ll need to schedule it within the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll call radiology. Any other follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular meds, including IVIG—your next dose is due soon. And keep your oncology follow-up. Call if you develop fever, severe pain, or stop passing stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your exam is normal, labs are stable, and you’ve tolerated regular food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So the obstruction is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it appears resolved. We don’t think it was cancer-related. But the MRE will help confirm everything’s moving properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really worried it was the lymphoma back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But right now, everything points to a temporary issue. Keep up with your specialists, and we’ll stay on top of any changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today because of a new headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about three days ago. It's in my right forehead and temple, and it gets worse as the day goes on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned it’s different from your usual migraines. Does anything make it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I’ve taken my regular pain meds, even the methadone, but it doesn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’ve been having this every morning when you wake up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s there when I wake up and just keeps building.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea, vision changes, or weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no weakness or blurry vision. But my doctor noticed my eyes were twitching to the right during my IVIG infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called nystagmus. Given your history of lymphoma in the brain, we need to rule out any recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I was worried about that too. Is that likely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we have to check for, but it’s not the most common cause. We’re going to get an MRI of your head tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your MRI results are back. The good news is your old brain lesion looks stable, and there are no new tumors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s such a relief!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we did see increased swelling and thickening in your right frontal sinus. That could be causing your headache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sinusitis? But I’ve been using my nasal spray and allergy meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but with your history of lymphoma, the neuro-oncology team wants us to do a lumbar puncture tomorrow to be sure there’s no lymphoma in the spinal fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that safe? I’ve never had one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very safe. We’ll use local numbing medicine. It’s mostly to rule out something serious, not because we think it’s likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When will we know the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It takes a few days. We’ll check cell counts, infection, and for any abnormal cells. Your oncologist will follow up with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about the headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat it as sinusitis for now. You’ll start an antibiotic called levofloxacin for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to sulfa and penicillin—will this be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, levofloxacin is safe for you. It’s not related to those antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had enough bad reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the headache today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less intense?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’re going to do the lumbar puncture in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I need to lie flat afterward?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have you lie flat for about an hour to reduce the chance of a spinal headache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lumbar puncture went well. We got a good sample and you can sit up now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much—just pressure. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The initial report says no white blood cells or bacteria were seen in the spinal fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection or lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection, which is excellent. The full test for lymphoma cells will take a few more days, but this is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your spinal fluid culture came back with no growth. Everything so far points to sinusitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re doing well. We’ll send you home with the antibiotic and instructions to follow up with your neuro-oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I was really scared it was the cancer coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your scans are stable, and your symptoms fit sinusitis. Keep taking the antibiotic and call if the headache worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call my oncologist to schedule the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having worsening right-sided headaches and eye pain. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few weeks ago. At first, I just had nystagmus when looking far to the right, but no pain. Now, when I look that way, my right eye and forehead hurt constantly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any changes in vision, numbness, or weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vision loss, but I’ve been using my reading glasses more. I have some numbness in my left leg, but that’s been stable since my back surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of lymphoma, we ordered an MRI urgently. It showed a new mass in your right nasopharynx and worsening sinus disease. We’re concerned it could be a recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. But I’ve been in remission for years. Could it be something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be infection or inflammation, but we can’t rule out lymphoma. ENT will do a biopsy tomorrow to find out. We’ll also check your bone marrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under general anesthesia, so you won’t feel anything. It’s important we get tissue to know what we’re dealing with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. What about my other conditions—diabetes, immune deficiency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing those too. Your IVIG dose was given today. For diabetes, we’re using insulin instead of your pills while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain meds—methadone, Dilaudid—are they okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued all your chronic meds. We’ll keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the biopsy this morning. The ENT team found purulent material and took tissue samples.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go? Did they see the mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s a mass in the right nasopharynx. They drained some infected fluid. Cultures are growing bacteria, so we’re starting antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bacteria? So it might not be cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be both. The mass is concerning for lymphoma, but there’s also a serious sinus infection. We’ll know more when the biopsy results come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What antibiotics are you giving me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin and Levaquin. The culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae and MRSA—resistant staph—so we need strong coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to penicillin and sulfa. Is this safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, vancomycin and Levaquin are safe for you. We checked your allergies carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tissue culture confirmed Streptococcus and MRSA. Sensitivities show vancomycin will work well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the infection is real. But what about the mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still waiting on the pathology. It may take a few days. We also did a CT of your torso to check for other lymph nodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my bone marrow biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s scheduled for day after tomorrow. It helps us see if there’s any lymphoma involvement there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRI of your orbits today to check if the mass is affecting your eye nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it? I’m worried about my vision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the optic nerves and eye muscles look normal. No sign of tumor spread there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My headache is a bit better since the antibiotics started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. The infection is likely contributing to your pain. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had your bone marrow biopsy this morning. It went well, and we sent the sample for testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any pain expected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some soreness, but it should fade. We’ll manage it with your usual pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count was low on admission, but it’s improving with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the infection or my immune deficiency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely both. Your CVID makes you prone to infections, and the current one may have worsened the pancytopenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. Your IgG level was normal. We’ll continue your regular schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The preliminary pathology shows CD30-positive cells. It’s not clear yet if it’s Hodgkin’s, PTLD, or something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here for you. Keep taking your meds, rest, and call if anything changes. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I came because my hearing suddenly dropped in my right ear about four days ago. It started like I was underwater, then felt like cotton was stuffed in it, and now I can’t hear anything. It’s painful too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any drainage from the ear or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No drainage, and I haven’t had a fever. But I’ve also been having this new pain that shoots down my left arm when I move my neck or shoulder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for letting me know. We’re also following up on that nasopharyngeal mass seen on your last CT. You don’t have sore throat or trouble swallowing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, my throat feels fine. No pain there. But I’m worried—could this be lymphoma coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. Your history makes us cautious, but your last PET scan and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Still, we’ll keep investigating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad those were clear. But this ear thing is really scaring me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The fluid in your middle ear is likely due to the mass pressing on the Eustachian tube. It’s not infected now, but it’s causing pressure and hearing loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an ear infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. No signs of bacterial infection. ENT will follow up after discharge to monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. What about the shoulder pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray today. It looked normal—no fracture or dislocation. But we’re ordering an MRI tomorrow to get a better look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be related to the lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but your oncologist thinks it’s more likely musculoskeletal. The MRI will help us decide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve been on a lot of meds—do I need to change anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your list. You’re on acyclovir, methadone, glimepiride, metformin, and others. We’ll keep them running as before unless something changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My blood sugar’s been a little high lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw your glucose was 295 this morning. We’ll monitor it and adjust insulin if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to do a biopsy of the nasopharyngeal mass today. It’s similar to the one you had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it necessary? I thought the last one was inconclusive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because the mass is still there. The earlier biopsy showed some atypical cells with CD30 and EBV markers, but no clear cancer. This time, we hope for more tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it’s not cancer, what else could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a reactive process—your immune system overresponding due to infection or inflammation, especially with your CVID.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy went well. They got a good sample. Pathology will take a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any fluid or pus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They found cystic fluid, but no malignant cells. It wasn’t sent for culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not an abscess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not clearly. The imaging suggested it, but the fluid didn’t look infected. You’re not on antibiotics now because you’re not febrile or systemically ill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We swabbed your throat yesterday to check for herpes or shingles. The results came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had mouth ulcers before—could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked. No HSV or VZV. Likely unrelated to the current issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your shoulder MRI is back. It shows tendinosis in the rotator cuff and some thickening of ligaments—consistent with adhesive capsulitis, or 'frozen shoulder.'

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lymphoma involvement. No joint infection either. It’s a strain, likely from overuse or posture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Physical therapy first. If that doesn’t help, your PCP can consider a steroid injection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pathology from the biopsy is still pending. But so far, no signs of active infection or clear malignancy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But they saw reactive cells?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a cluster of reactive cells that look suspicious, but not diagnostic. We’ll need follow-up with ENT and oncology to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not in danger now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable. No fever, no worsening symptoms. That’s why we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. ENT will see you for the ear fluid and mass. And your oncologist will review the biopsy results when they’re final.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. Keep taking everything as before. And please keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. If your hearing doesn’t improve or the shoulder pain worsens, call your doctor right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I feel much better just knowing it’s not an active infection or cancer right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. The nurse will go over discharge instructions and get you ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your blood counts are still low, but stable. That’s likely from your CVID and past treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I’ve had that for years. As long as it’s not getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll monitor it with your regular doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch if anything changes with your results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve had diarrhea and right lower belly pain for a few days. My ostomy’s been very active—loose and non-bloody. The pain’s not too bad now, but it was worse earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, nausea, or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or vomiting. I feel tired, but not sick like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I see you were at the hematology clinic today for your IVIG and they sent you here because of the pain and diarrhea. They gave you two antibiotics—cefepime and flagyl—just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they were worried it might be an infection or something related to my lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ve reviewed your CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis. It didn’t show any infection, appendicitis, or bowel issue. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s good. So it’s not my lymphoma coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of recurrence on the scan. Your lymph nodes and spleen are the same size as before. We also did a chest CT, and those nodules and nodes are stable too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why the pain and diarrhea then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely a viral gastroenteritis. Several family members had similar symptoms, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my sister and nephew had diarrhea last week. They’re better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That supports the idea of a virus. Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no bacteria. But what about the blood work? I saw my counts were low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have pancytopenia—low white blood cells, hemoglobin, and platelets. This has been happening over time. It could be due to viral suppression of your bone marrow, not necessarily lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be my immune deficiency affecting this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CVID may play a role, but we think the virus is the main trigger right now. We’ll monitor your counts after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my sodium? I saw it dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your sodium is now 131. It was 140 on admission. This is likely from the IV fluids you got. You’re not showing symptoms, so we’ll watch it and recheck as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m glad it’s not serious. Do I need more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. You only needed that one dose since we don’t think it’s a bacterial infection. We’ll hold off on more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The pain is much less, and my ostomy output has slowed down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs this morning show your white count and hemoglobin are still low, but we expected that. No new concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool virus test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Came back negative—no virus isolated. But that doesn’t rule out a viral cause. Sometimes tests miss it, especially if you’re already recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the CMV test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CMV was not detected. That’s good news. We also checked EBV, HHV6, and parvovirus—results pending, but we’ll follow up at your clinic visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my iron? I remember my ferritin was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your ferritin was very low at 10. You received an iron infusion yesterday—ferric gluconate. We’ll recheck your iron studies as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been worried about everything at once—lymphoma, counts, infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But right now, everything points to a viral illness causing temporary issues. Your lymphoma remains in remission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re doing well—pain is minimal, output is back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular medications. You have a follow-up in the hematology clinic in two days to check your blood counts and review all the test results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they check my sodium and iron again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll repeat your CBC, basic metabolic panel, and iron studies. Also, they’ll follow up on the viral tests—EBV, CMV, etc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my counts don’t improve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If they stay low, we may need to investigate further, but for now, we expect them to recover as you get over this illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I feel much better knowing it’s not my cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You responded well, and we’re confident this was a viral issue. Just keep an eye on your symptoms and call if you develop fever, severe pain, or increased diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I restart my IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your next Hizentra dose is scheduled for next week. Continue as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. Take care, and see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your pain meds. But call us if pain isn’t controlled, or if you develop fever, weakness, numbness, or bowel/bladder issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my lymphoma—any concern it came back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of recurrence. You’re still in remission. Continue your follow-ups with oncology as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send your discharge instructions and meds. Your mother will help you settle in. Take care, and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—your discharge meds are ready. You’ve got hydrocodone, acetaminophen, docusate, senna, and all your regulars like metformin and levothyroxine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the methadone included? I need it four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, methadone 5 mg four times daily is on the list. And acyclovir for herpes prevention, loratadine for allergies, and duloxetine for nerve pain and mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to run out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We made sure everything’s covered. You’re cleared to go home with services. Take it easy, and follow up in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your discharge paperwork is complete. You’re officially discharged as of now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve had bad stomach cramps and diarrhea for about a month now. It started after I saw some sick kids and then got my IVIG infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how frequent are the stools? Any blood or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A few times a day, liquid at first, but they’re starting to firm up. I had red stools once after red jello, but no more since. No fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. Given your history of lymphoma and immune deficiency, we want to be careful. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been feeling dizzy when I stand up. Started a few days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was low in clinic—94 over 55. That could explain the dizziness. We’ll monitor that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my left shoulder’s been hurting for about a week. Was I supposed to get an X-ray before coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it wasn’t done. We’ll order that tomorrow so we can check it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’m just worried it’s something serious with my lymphoma coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your symptoms are more likely due to an infection, especially since others around you were sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been trying to eat more carbs to firm up my stools, but it’s just made my blood sugar worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw your HbA1c is 7%, so diabetes is under reasonable control. We’ll hold your metformin for now and use insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. What about my IVIG? I’m due for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give it during your stay. It’s important for your immune deficiency. We’ll also start antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to penicillin and sulfa drugs. Just so you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. You already got cefepime and flagyl in clinic, which are safe for you. We’ll continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan from yesterday didn’t show any new masses or bowel issues. Lymph nodes are stable, and your spleen is slightly larger but unchanged from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s blocking or inflamed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the scan looks clear. That’s reassuring. Your shoulder X-ray is also normal—no fracture or arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt? Could it be lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but unlikely. We’ll keep an eye on it. You may need an MRI later if it doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. How’s my blood work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is low—2.2—because of your immune condition. Hemoglobin is a bit low too, but stable. Platelets are okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. Your levels are consistent with your history. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling your colonoscopy for today. It’s mostly to rule out infection or inflammation since your symptoms haven’t fully resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they take biopsies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll take a few samples. It might help us find a cause if it’s not just a virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my IVIG? Is that still happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after the colonoscopy. You’re getting your full dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy was unremarkable. The inside of your bowel looks healthy. No ulcers, masses, or active inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No sign of lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No visible signs. Biopsies are pending, but so far, nothing concerning. We also tested for C. diff and parasites—both negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the CMV test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CMV came back negative. So it’s not that either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely a lingering viral or bacterial gastroenteritis. Your immune deficiency makes it harder to clear infections quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics will help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, cipro and flagyl cover a broad range of bacteria. We’ll send you home with a full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s improved, right? We think it was due to dehydration from diarrhea. Your blood pressure is still low but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel less lightheaded now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your ostomy site looks better too—less red than when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re feeling better, stools are firmer, and no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds, plus cipro and flagyl for a week. Also, loperamide for diarrhea and dicyclomine for cramps if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid? I know it’s limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 18 tablets. Please discuss with your pain doctor about long-term use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Any follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We ordered a strongyloides IgG test—important for someone on IVIG. And please follow up on the colonoscopy biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my shoulder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it doesn’t get better, your doctor may order an MRI. But for now, it’s likely musculoskeletal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. When should I call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, worsening pain, more diarrhea, or blood in stool—call right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? Should I restart metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart it tomorrow. Just monitor your sugars closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be out by noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, all good. Stomach feels better, and I’m not dizzy anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember to follow up with your primary doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. I understand you came in with neck and head pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started after my lymph node biopsy. It’s sharp, constant pain from the top of my head down to my collarbone on the right side. It’s about a 7 out of 10.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned headaches and vision changes too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the headaches are different—worse with light. And I’ve had three times where I completely lost vision in my right eye for a few seconds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. We’ll need to do an MRI to see what’s going on. Your blood work shows low white blood cells and anemia, so we’ll keep an eye on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having ear drainage too. My ENT said I have a perforated eardrum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. We’ll continue the ofloxacin drops and keep the ear dry. We’re also starting you on cefepime, just in case there’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI results are back. There’s been a big increase in the size of a mass in your nasopharynx. It’s spreading into nearby areas, including the skull base and nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The recent biopsy confirmed Hodgkin lymphoma, and this mass appears to be part of that. It’s likely causing your pain and vision issues due to nerve involvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the chemotherapy help shrink it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting ICE chemotherapy today. It’s designed to treat aggressive lymphomas. We’ll also consider intrathecal methotrexate to protect your nervous system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already on antibiotics. Is the fever from infection or the lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your fever could be from either. Your cultures haven’t grown anything yet, so we’re watching closely. The cefepime is a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling a lumbar puncture tomorrow. We need to check if the lymphoma has reached your spinal fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my back surgery history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll use fluoroscopy to guide the needle safely. It’s important to rule out central nervous system involvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. My pain is still bad—can we adjust my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted pain management. They recommend increasing your Lyrica to 50 mg four times a day. We’ll also keep your dilaudid and methadone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT and orbit MRI confirm the mass is pressing on nerves near your eye and skull. No new brain lesions, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the vision loss might stop if the tumor shrinks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the hope. Ophthalmology checked your eyes—no swelling or damage. The vision loss is likely from nerve compression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lumbar puncture went well. We gave intrathecal methotrexate. The fluid had some blood, so it’s hard to say if there are cancer cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s inconclusive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re treating as if there’s a risk. The methotrexate helps prevent spread. Your cell counts are low, so we’ve started Neupogen to help them recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been more tired and my mouth hurts. Is that from chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, mucositis is common. We’ve started magic mouthwash and nystatin. We also added fluconazole in case it’s fungal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You seemed more drowsy yesterday. We think the fluconazole might be interacting with your methadone. We’ve stopped fluconazole and started micafungin instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel more alert today. Is the micafungin safer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it still covers fungal infections. Your mouth sores are improving, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has been high. The steroids we gave are making it worse. We’ve started insulin to manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m usually on pills. Can I go back to them after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll transition you back. But for now, insulin gives us better control, especially with the steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got your IVIG today—50 grams. Your immunoglobulin levels are stable, which helps your immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about infections with my low counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. That’s why you’re on acyclovir and atovaquone for prevention. Your blood cultures are still negative—no sign of active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped, so we gave a unit of red blood cells. You have microcytic anemia—likely iron deficiency. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Should I take iron at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss that with your oncologist. For now, transfusions are safest given your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You spiked a fever last night. We restarted cefepime. It’s likely due to low neutrophils from chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that delay my treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see how you respond. The ICE cycle is complete, so we’re focusing on recovery now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your fever is gone, and blood cultures are negative. We’re stopping cefepime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My headache is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The steroids and chemo are helping reduce inflammation. Your neck exam shows the lymph node is smaller.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge. You’ll continue atovaquone and all your home meds, including the new Lyrica dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your oncologist in a week. Also, neuro-ophthalmology to check your vision. Keep monitoring your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is improving. Platelets are still low, so avoid injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. Can I travel for appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but have someone with you. And call us if you develop fever, worsening pain, or vision changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging tomorrow. Continue the ofloxacin drops for your ear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes meds—back to glimepiride and metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart them. We’ll send instructions to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really scared with the vision loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’ve responded well to treatment. The mass is likely shrinking, and your symptoms are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your vitals are stable, pain is controlled, and you’re eating well. Discharge is set for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Will I need another IVIG soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last dose was this week, so next is in about four weeks. Your immunology team will coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my colostomy—everything looks okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your ostomy is healthy, and output is normal. Keep up with your care routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Here’s your discharge summary. Keep all your follow-ups, take your meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your oncology team members. I’ll be checking in on you during this admission. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a bit tired, but okay. My neck still hurts, and I’ve been worried about starting the second round of chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re here for your second cycle of R-ICE chemotherapy, which we’re starting tomorrow. The good news is your last MRI showed the nasopharyngeal mass has shrunk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s good to hear. But why are we adding Rituxan this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your recent EBV viral load was elevated. Since you have CVID, your immune system can’t control EBV well, and it may be driving the lymphoma. Rituxan helps target those abnormal B cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, okay. That makes sense. Will it make me feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some patients feel a little flu-like during the first infusion, but we’ll give you pre-medications to help. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My back’s been aching too—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got an MRI of your lumbar spine today to check. It showed only your known degenerative changes from your prior surgery—no signs of lymphoma spreading there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was scared it might be cancer again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’re being extra cautious because of your history. Your spleen is a bit larger than before, but that’s common with lymphoma activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my blood counts? Last time I was really low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is low at 1.5, and hemoglobin is 7.5, so we’ll keep an eye on it. We’ll transfuse if your hemoglobin drops below 7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It helped me feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We also adjusted your diabetes meds. We’re using insulin now instead of your oral meds because steroids can raise blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I forgot I’m on dexamethasone with this chemo. My sugars have been high at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your glucose four times a day and giving insulin as needed. Once you’re home, we’ll restart your glimepiride and metformin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain? I’m on methadone and dilaudid, but sometimes it’s not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team reviewed your meds. We’re keeping your current doses. Pregabalin was increased last time and seems to be helping with nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it has. My headaches are better too—probably from the chemo shrinking the mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s a good sign the treatment is working. We’ll keep monitoring with scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today we’ll start your R-ICE chemo, including Rituxan. It’ll take a few hours. Any questions before we begin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Will I lose my hair again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely, yes. But it will grow back after treatment ends. We can talk about scalp cooling if you’re interested.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe later. I just want to get through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. The nurse will start the infusion now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any nausea or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little nauseated, but the ondansetron helps. No fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your white count is up to 2.0 today, which is improving. We’ll keep giving antibiotics to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still on acyclovir and atovaquone, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both continue. They help protect you from infections because of your CVID.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my IVIG? When’s my next dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get it in clinic in about two weeks. Your last level was good, so we’re keeping it every four weeks as you prefer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not come more often. It’s a long trip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll monitor your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow you’ll get intrathecal methotrexate via lumbar puncture to protect your central nervous system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It was uncomfortable, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use fluoroscopy to guide the needle, and you’ll be awake but relaxed. We’ll collect some fluid to check for lymphoma cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll feel pressure, but we’ll numb the area first. Most patients tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lumbar puncture went smoothly. We gave the methotrexate and sent the fluid for testing. No immediate issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I feel okay—just a little stiff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep you lying flat for a bit to reduce headache risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? That’s great. What about the Neupogen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get your first dose before you leave. You’ll inject it daily at home to help your white count recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve done it before. I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Continue all your usual meds, including methadone, clonazepam, and your inhaler.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your oncologist in a week, and your IVIG is scheduled in two weeks. Call us if you develop fever, severe pain, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I feel like I’m on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep up the strength. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my hearing. It’s still not great since the ear surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. ENT said the tube is in place and the infection is cleared. The hearing loss may be from long-term inflammation, but they’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep using the ofloxacin drops as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’m ready to go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. Your walker is here, and a nurse will go over your meds one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for everything. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was our pleasure. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your oncology team members. We’ve admitted you today for your third cycle of R-ICE chemotherapy. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay—just the usual sinus pain, nothing new. I’m a bit tired, but my appetite’s been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, no fevers or chills? Any nausea or abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just the chronic sinus pressure. I’ve had it for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll keep monitoring. Your blood counts came back low again—WBC 2.1, hemoglobin 8.7, platelets 63. That’s expected with R-ICE, but we’ll watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ve been low before. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s expected, not dangerous right now. We’ll give your chemotherapy and support your counts. You’ve tolerated it well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been using my home meds as usual—methadone, Dilaudid, all of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your home medications. We held metformin and glimepiride during admission but will restart them later with insulin coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been high lately. Is that from the steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Dexamethasone can raise blood sugar. We’re on a sliding scale insulin for now. We’ll watch it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also scheduled an MRI of your nasopharynx this afternoon to check how the skull base mass is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. The last one showed improvement, didn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, after two cycles, there was a clear decrease in size. We’re hopeful this one shows more progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your MRI results are back. Good news—the mass in your skull base has decreased further. No new brain lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean the chemo is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s responding well. The asymmetry and enhancement are still there, but much improved. We’ll continue with R-ICE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hearing loss? Still from the eustachian tube blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fluid in the mastoids due to the mass pressing on the tube. No infection seen. ENT is monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your R-ICE chemo today. It includes rituximab, ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide, plus dexamethasone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rituximab again? Because of the EBV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your EBV viral load was elevated, so we added rituximab to target those infected cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fatigue, nausea, low blood counts. Ifosfamide can cause drowsiness—we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight. But you were a bit drowsy this morning—any confusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt really sleepy. Like I couldn’t focus. But I’m clearer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely from ifosfamide. It can cause temporary somnolence. Good that it’s improving. No weakness or numbness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just sleepy. My back pain is the same—still managed with meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
