conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your pain regimen. Your hemoglobin dropped to 7.3, so we’ll give one unit of red blood cells today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I remember needing that last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, anemia is common with chemo and your history. It’s not dangerous—we’re just supporting you through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood counts are still low—WBC 1.6, platelets 50. But stable. No fever or infection signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another platelet transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll watch. You’re not bleeding, so we can wait. Your body just needs time to recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And after this cycle? What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discussing transplant options—possibly allogeneic, given your poor marrow reserve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds intense. Is it necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a possibility, not a plan yet. We’ll evaluate after this cycle and see if your counts recover enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’ll start filgrastim at home to help your white count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have it at home. How long do I use it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Daily until your follow-up. We’ll decide then if you need more. Also, keep checking your blood sugar twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because of the dexamethasone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your last fingerstick was 320. If it stays over 300, call your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds—everything goes back to normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds resume—methadone, Dilaudid, acyclovir, atovaquone, and your thyroid and diabetes pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And IVIG? I’m due soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re scheduled for IVIG in four weeks. We’ll coordinate with your immunology team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Follow up with Dr. Patel in one week for blood work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel okay—tired, but no new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Keep using filgrastim, check sugars, and call if you feel feverish or worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see you all next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad the tumor is shrinking and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest up and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted last night with blood and mucus from your rectum and black stool from your stoma. Can you tell me more about when this started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about a day ago. I had right lower quadrant pain and noticed blood and mucus when I emptied my pouch. Then I saw black stool come through my stoma once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You recently finished your third cycle of R-ICE chemotherapy. We’re concerned this could be an infection or inflammation in your bowel. We’ve ordered a CT scan and will likely do a scope to check your rectum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it related to the lymphoma coming back? I’ve been so worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, we don’t think it’s a relapse. Your recent PET scan showed FDG-avid nodes, but the bleeding is more likely due to infection or irritation from your colostomy. We’ll test for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan shows wall thickening in the rectosigmoid stump with inflammation—consistent with proctitis. We’ll do a flexible sigmoidoscopy today to get biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt? I’ve had a lot of procedures lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so it shouldn’t be uncomfortable. We need to rule out infections like CMV or C. diff, which are more common after chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scope is done. We saw ulceration and inflammation in the pouch. Biopsies were taken. No pseudomembranes, so it’s less likely to be severe C. diff, but we’re sending stool tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the biopsies? How long will that take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A few days for full results. But we’re already treating you with vancomycin by mouth just in case it’s C. diff, since that’s common in your situation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the stool test came back positive for C. diff. That explains the bleeding and pain. We’ll continue oral vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’ve heard it can be serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with low immunity. But we caught it early. You’re not having diarrhea or fever, so it’s mild. We’ll keep you here until your white count improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugar has been high since I got here. It was usually under control with pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we stopped your oral meds because of the infection. We’ve started insulin. After your IVIG infusion, your sugars spiked—possibly due to insulin antibodies. We’ve restarted metformin and adjusted your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I felt really resistant to insulin. Is it safe to restart metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your kidney function is good. We’re also using a low-carb supplement. Your sugars have improved, though we had one low—72—so we adjusted the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your biopsy results are back. It’s chronic active colitis, but CMV is negative. Given your CVID, it’s likely diversion colitis or infection. Since C. diff is confirmed, we’ll focus on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s diversion colitis? I’ve never heard of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When part of the bowel is bypassed, like with your colostomy, the unused segment can get inflamed. It’s not dangerous, but can cause bleeding. We’d normally use enemas, but with low platelets, it’s too risky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is dropping—now 1.9. We’re continuing filgrastim to help it recover. This also increases your infection risk, so we’re keeping you in isolation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so tired. Is that from the low counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your hemoglobin is down to 8.3. You’ve lost blood from the colitis. We gave four units of red cells, and your levels are stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have these sores in my mouth and on my stoma. Are they from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are mucositis—common with chemo. We’ll keep using mouth rinses and stoma care. It should improve as your counts recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You received your IVIG today. We’re keeping it to every four weeks, as you prefer. It helps with your CVID and may reduce infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I know it’s important, but coming every three weeks was too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain flared up yesterday. We think it’s from mucositis, not worsening C. diff. We’ve started metronidazole for 14 days to cover any bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the sores too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Indirectly. It reduces gut bacteria that can irritate the lining. The sores themselves will heal as your immune system recovers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray today shows no pneumonia or fluid. Heart size is normal. Port is in good position. This is reassuring before your transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still scheduled for transplant? I thought this admission might delay it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as long as your infection is under control and counts improve. We’ve cleared your dental work and sent all pre-transplant labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious—worried the lymphoma is back or I won’t make it to transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Your depression and anxiety are being managed with duloxetine and clonazepam. We can adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HBV test came back negative. That’s good—we needed to confirm before transplant. All other infection screens are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelets dropped to 11, and you had another small bleed. We gave a platelet transfusion, and it stopped. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared of bleeding. Will this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unlikely once your counts recover. The C. diff and inflammation are the main triggers. As those improve, your risk goes down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI of the nasopharynx shows the skull base mass is smaller, and lymph nodes are shrinking. No new brain lesions. Your Hodgkin’s is responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about the headaches and hearing loss earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ENT found no lymphoma in the ear biopsies—just inflammation. The mass is improving with treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed the 14-day course of metronidazole. We’ll continue oral vancomycin until transplant to prevent C. diff recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll take it at home? How long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, until you’re readmitted for transplant. It’s a precaution. Your counts are slowly rising, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat MRI confirms the trend—your nasopharyngeal mass is continuing to shrink. No new concerns in the brain. You’re on track for transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. I’m feeling stronger every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is still low but stable. Hemoglobin is holding. We’ll discharge you tomorrow if you stay symptom-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, worsening abdominal pain, or bloody stools. Keep taking vancomycin, insulin, and your other meds. Use glucose gel if your sugar drops below 70.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My back pain is flaring. Can I have my usual methadone and dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your methadone and cyclobenzaprine. Use dilaudid as needed. We’ll keep lyrica and pregabalin for nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No fever, pain, or bleeding. We’re discharging you home. You’ll see Dr. Evans on the 5th to finalize transplant plans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so worried when I came in. I feel much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You handled this well. Keep up with your appointments, take your meds, and call if anything changes. We’ll see you soon for transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more chemo before transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’ve completed three cycles of R-ICE. The plan is to proceed directly to transplant, given your remission and the risks of more chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? Should I keep the insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue glargine and the sliding scale. We’ll reassess after transplant. Keep using the low-carb supplement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin? Until I’m readmitted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take it four times a day. It’s to prevent C. diff from coming back before your immune system recovers post-transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I restart the duloxetine daily? You changed it to 20mg once a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take one 20mg capsule daily. We lowered it due to nausea, but if you’re tolerating it, it should help with mood and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my clonazepam for anxiety?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue 1mg four times a day as needed. We’ll follow up with your psychiatrist after transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. Rest, stay hydrated, and call us with any concerns. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I know you’re here for your stem cell transplant. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Dr. Lee. I’m a little anxious, but otherwise okay. I just want to get through this transplant safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’re going to take good care of you. First, we’ll place a central line so we can give your medications and draw blood easily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. The one in my neck? Is it the same kind?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a triple-lumen catheter in your left internal jugular. It’s already been placed successfully. You’ll have it for the whole stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start your conditioning chemotherapy tomorrow—fludarabine and busulfan. It prepares your body to accept the donor stem cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the transplant itself? When does that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s scheduled for day 6 of your admission—so around May 17th. The stem cells will be infused through your central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I’m still on vancomycin for C. diff—will I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your oral vancomycin throughout your stay because of your weakened immune system. We don’t want the infection to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My blood sugars have been high lately—will that be watched?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the diabetes team will help manage that. You’re already on insulin and metformin, and we’ll adjust doses as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re starting your chemotherapy today—fludarabine and busulfan. This will last a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fatigue, nausea, and low blood counts are common. We’ll monitor you closely. We’ve also started prophylactic medications to prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like the atovaquone and acyclovir I take at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re on those, plus others to prevent lung infections and herpes reactivation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white count is dropping, which is expected. We’ve started filgrastim to help your neutrophils recover later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m more at risk for infections now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, so we’re keeping you in protective isolation. No fresh flowers or raw foods, and we’ll screen visitors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been a bit nauseous. Is that from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. We’ll increase your ondansetron and add another anti-nausea med. Make sure to drink fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood counts are very low, as expected. No signs of infection so far—your CMV test was negative today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been worried about CMV with my immune deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring weekly. You’re also on fluconazole to prevent fungal infections, which we’ll continue after transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day—we’re going to infuse your donor stem cells. You’ve been randomized to a study with tacrolimus, sirolimus, and bortezomib to prevent graft-versus-host disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel anything during the infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most patients don’t. We’ll monitor your vital signs closely. The stem cells will find their way to your bone marrow and start making new blood cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infusion went smoothly. You did great. We’ll keep an eye on you for any reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay, but my ostomy output has been watery. Should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned it might be early graft-versus-host disease in the gut. We’re starting budesonide to help calm the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve heard GVHD can be bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is mild and treatable. We’re catching it early. Most patients respond well to budesonide. We’ll watch your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your neutrophil count is starting to rise. That’s a sign your transplant is engrafting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a very positive sign. Your body is starting to make new blood cells. We’ll keep supporting you until your counts normalize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My right eye feels blurry. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve referred you to ophthalmology. It could be a cataract or something related to your transplant. We’ll get an MRI to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI of your brain and orbits is back. No new lymphoma or orbital mass. There is a cataract, which explains the blurry vision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not cancer? That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, no signs of lymphoma recurrence. The changes in your nasopharynx are stable and likely inflammatory.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugars have been high again. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, steroids and stress can raise them. The diabetes team adjusted your insulin—now 50 units of glargine at dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep checking them. Any update on my tacrolimus level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was a bit high, so we reduced your dose to 0.5 mg twice a day. We’ll recheck it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest blood cultures are negative—no infection. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my C. diff test? Still negative?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll keep you on vancomycin for now to prevent recurrence, given your immune status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is clear—no pneumonia. You’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having more back pain. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give IV dilaudid for breakthrough pain. We’ve kept your methadone and lyrica going, but we’ll adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is now 5.0—excellent! You’ve engrafted successfully. We’re stopping filgrastim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We want to make sure your counts stay stable and your diarrhea improves before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV is still negative, and your stool test showed no virus. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the budesonide—is it helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your ostomy output has normalized. We’ll keep you on budesonide at home and monitor for GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled your discharge for June 4th. You’ll go home on tacrolimus, sirolimus, budesonide, and vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So many meds. Will I need to stay on them forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not forever. We’ll taper them over time. The vancomycin and antivirals may continue for a few months due to your immune deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Hemoglobin is 8.9, platelets 40,000. We won’t need to transfuse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? Will I stay on insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll work with endocrinology to adjust as your recovery continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your discharge plan. You’ll have labs drawn tomorrow and tacrolimus/sirolimus levels checked in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with transplant, oncology, and your primary team. We’ll make sure everything’s coordinated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning! You’re doing great. We’re finalizing your discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—how will I know if something goes wrong at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have fever, worsening diarrhea, shortness of breath, or blood sugar below 80 or above 300. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. We’re proud of your progress. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with a fever and cough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had a fever a few days ago, but it went down with Tylenol. I’ve been coughing more and my sinuses feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some blood around your stoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I think I might have torn it changing the bag. But there’s still a pocket of blood under it. I’m also noticing I bleed longer from my fingersticks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Your immune system is still recovering from the transplant, so we need to be careful about infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on antibiotics before for lung issues. Could this be something like that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest CT showed some new cavitary lesions—areas that could suggest infection, possibly fungal or bacterial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fungal? Like from mold or something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But we also need to rule out other things like tuberculosis, especially given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was treated for latent TB years ago. Could it come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Quantiferon test before transplant was negative, so reactivation is less likely, but we can’t rule it out completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a bronchoscopy tomorrow to get samples from your lungs. That will help us identify what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. It’s very safe and will give us critical information.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. I just want to make sure it’s not my lymphoma coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your recent PET scan didn’t show active lymphoma. These lung changes are more likely infection-related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been through so much already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We got some early results from your blood and sputum. No TB was seen, and blood cultures are negative so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. What about the bronchoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for today. We’ll get fluid from your lungs to test for bacteria, fungi, and viruses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stoma? Should I be worried about the blood pocket?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We examined it—it looks clean. The bleeding may be due to low platelets. Your count is low, which is common after transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it should get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as your counts recover. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bronchoscopy went well. We collected samples. Preliminary gram stain shows some staph bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Staph? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but the good news is it’s not MRSA. It’s sensitive to vancomycin and trimethoprim-sulfa, so treatable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But why did I get it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your immune system is still suppressed from the transplant and medications like tacrolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not the lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the lung findings are due to infection. Your Hodgkin’s is still in remission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Final results are back. The bronchial fluid grew Staph aureus, but no TB, fungus, or viruses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just a bacterial infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re discharging you with a 7-day course of levofloxacin, even though the bacteria is resistant, because it’s mild and you're improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, resistant? Shouldn’t I get something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. The infection is clearing, and levofloxacin is being used short-term. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my prednisone? I’m down to 2.5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the 3-day taper and stop. Your GVHD is stable on budesonide, tacrolimus, and sirolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Insulin, methadone, all of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your regular medications are continued. We added lamivudine for hepatitis B, even though you’re not positive, as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I had hepatitis B.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You don’t. But with your immune status, we’re being cautious in case of reactivation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your oncologist next week. We’ll check your tacrolimus and sirolimus levels then. Also, get an ultrasound of your port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on it. If the blood pocket grows or becomes painful, call your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Keep taking the levofloxacin, watch for fever, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted because of a lung infection. Can I go over what we know so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I’ve been so tired and short of breath. I was worried it was my lymphoma coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your recent scans and tests don’t show lymphoma activity. We did a bronchoscopy earlier, and the fluid from your lungs grew Staphylococcus aureus — that’s what’s causing the pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Staph? Is that serious? I’ve had infections before since the transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your immune system being weaker. But we’re treating it with vancomycin, which works well against this type of staph. You’re already on it through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my breathing? I feel better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your oxygen levels are stable on room air, and your lungs sound clear. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re definitely improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been so anxious lately. I stopped my duloxetine before coming in — my oncologist said it might affect my blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain some of the mood swings and agitation you’ve had. We’re keeping you on clonazepam for now. We’ll talk more about restarting duloxetine before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been tearful and just overwhelmed. I didn’t mean to snap at the nurse earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You don’t need to apologize. We know this is a lot. We’ll make sure you have support when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work shows your white count is low — 1.4 — which isn’t unexpected given your history. But it means we have to be extra careful about infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m still on isolation precautions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. But since your sputum tests didn’t show TB or fungus, we don’t need negative pressure isolation. You’re safe to have visitors as long as they wash hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My cousin wants to visit. And what about my kidney numbers? My creatinine was high yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine was 1.1. It may be from the vancomycin. We’re giving you IV fluids to protect your kidneys and will adjust the dose if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard vancomycin can be rough on kidneys. Will I be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. Your levels improved today — creatinine down to 0.9. That’s a good sign the fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your vancomycin level back — it was high at 11.4. We’ve lowered the dose to avoid toxicity, especially for your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll stay on the lower dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1000 mg once daily. You’ll finish the two-week course at home with a visiting nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant meds — tacrolimus and sirolimus — are those okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your levels are in range. We’ll keep checking them twice a week. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a cardiac MRI yesterday to check for any infection spread — endocarditis. The result came back normal. No mass on the heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was so worried about that. Thank you for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Better safe than sorry. Your spleen is a bit enlarged, but that’s been seen before and isn’t new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? It’s been high. I’m on insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve adjusted your sliding scale. Your fasting sugars are coming down. We held metformin while you’re in the hospital — safer with the IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your CMV test came back negative. That means we don’t need to add antiviral treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been scared of CMV since my transplant. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also keeping an eye on your anemia. Your hemoglobin is 8.2. We’ll transfuse if it drops below 7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get tired easily. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. But also from the infection and everything your body’s been through. You’re on iron supplements and folic acid to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’re afebrile, breathing well, and your labs are stabilizing. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What will I need at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A visiting nurse will come daily to give your vancomycin IV and check your kidney function. You’ll also get IV fluids to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds — can I restart everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications will continue. We’re adding duloxetine back at 20 mg twice daily for your mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I really need help with the anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged outpatient follow-up with your oncologist, psychiatrist, and home health. Call us if you develop fever, shortness of breath, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check — your labs are stable. Hemoglobin 8.2, creatinine 0.9, vancomycin level 11.7 — all acceptable for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stoma? It’s been okay, but I worry about infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ostomy site looks healthy. Keep using budesonide as prescribed — it helps with mild GVHD symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? I still use my albuterol sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your asthma is stable. Continue fluticasone and albuterol as needed. No wheezing today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better than when I came in. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Just take it easy at home and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll leave with instructions, prescriptions, and a nurse visit scheduled for this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drive myself home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend someone drive you. You’re on pain meds and it’s a long day with infusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My cousin can pick me up. And my IV meds — how long will I need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Seven more days. The nurse will coordinate the last dose and remove the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health — should I see someone sooner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your psychiatrist will see you in three days. Keep using clonazepam as needed, but don’t exceed the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had thoughts of not wanting to go on — but no plan. I’m scared I’ll get sick again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. You’ve been through so much. Please call your therapist or us if those thoughts return. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re strong, and you’re in remission from lymphoma. This pneumonia was a setback, but you’ve handled it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will. One step at a time. Let’s get you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will review your discharge instructions one more time, including med schedule and warning signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll read everything carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your fever goes above 100.4, or you have chest pain or trouble breathing, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And if my IV site gets red or swollen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call home health right away. They’ll assess and let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. For everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. Maybe watch a movie and just relax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s the best medicine right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it one day at a time. You’ve come so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Let the nurse know when you’re ready to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, I hope — as an outpatient!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. And I’ll make sure it’s for a check-up, not another admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll keep fighting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’ll keep supporting you. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today because of bleeding from your ostomy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started this morning around 8. It was constant for hours—my clothes were soaked. I’ve had small spots before, but never like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned feeling lightheaded and fatigued. Any dizziness when standing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, yes. But I didn’t pass out or anything. My clinic vitals were stable, they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. The surgical team evaluated you in the ER and found the bleeding at the base of the stoma, where it meets the skin. They applied a hemostatic agent called Surgicel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So it’s not coming from inside the bowel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s from the skin edge, likely due to irritation or minor trauma. But your platelet count is low, which can make bleeding harder to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My platelets are low again? I thought they were improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your platelets were 43,000—below normal. That’s why we gave you two units of platelets. The bleeding stopped after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it stopped. I was really scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. The ostomy nurse also helped refit your bag to reduce irritation. They noticed you were pulling the stoma up to look at it—can increase trauma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was just trying to see where it was coming from. I didn’t realize that could make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common instinct, but it can cause more bleeding. Try to avoid touching or pulling it. Let it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You also mentioned your stool has been watery and more frequent. Is that still happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had to empty the bag more often. It’s not full, but the output is loose and smells bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool for infections like C. diff, Salmonella, and parasites. The C. diff test came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had C. diff before. Could it come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but the test is negative now. Your diarrhea improved today, so we’ll monitor. Other tests are pending but so far no pathogens found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been on a low-bacteria diet, so I wasn’t sure what caused it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your transplant and immune deficiency, we’re being extra cautious. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I also see your tacrolimus level was a bit low—4.9. We’ve increased your dose from 1.5 mg to 2 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that for the transplant? I know it’s important to keep levels stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It helps prevent graft rejection. We’ll check the level again at your next follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to take it on time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray was clear, and you’re not having fevers or shortness of breath. Your recent MRSA pneumonia seems resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have a dry cough, but no fever. I’m glad the pneumonia isn’t back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cough may linger. We’ll keep monitoring, but no signs of infection now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs show your hemoglobin is stable, and platelets improved to 48,000.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. And the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool is back to normal—no more watery output. All infection tests came back negative except C. diff, which was already negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was probably just irritation or something temporary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. With your history, we wanted to rule out serious causes. But everything looks stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling much better. Do you think I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you stay stable, yes. We’ll discharge you tomorrow. We’ll send extra platelets home with you as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your oncologist tomorrow morning. We’ve increased your tacrolimus, so they’ll monitor levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ostomy? Should I see a specialist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ostomy nurse will call you at home to check in. Avoid pulling on the stoma. Use the supplies we gave you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home. Your ostomy isn’t bleeding, labs are stable, and diarrhea resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really worried yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. Just remember: no pulling on the stoma, take your meds, and follow up tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the walker you ordered?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s being sent to your house. It’s for stability, especially with your back pain and neuropathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been a bit unsteady lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring your transplant and lymphoma. But for now, focus on healing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you have any concerns—especially bleeding, fever, or diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve had two falls in the past two weeks. One while carrying a TV, and another going downstairs in slippers. I also keep falling asleep standing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you hit your head during the falls?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I hit my head, but I didn’t lose consciousness. My mom says I fell asleep while cooking dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. You mentioned fatigue and sleepiness. Any dizziness or chest pain with the falls?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no dizziness or chest pain. Just really tired and sleepy all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your blood work and do a CT scan of your head to make sure there’s no new issue from your past lymphoma or the fall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m on a lot of medications. Could that be part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. Some of your meds—like methadone, clonazepam, and dronabinol—can cause drowsiness, especially when combined.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking them as prescribed. My duloxetine was recently increased to 20 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll review all your meds. The fatigue and falls may be due to polypharmacy—too many sedating drugs together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could the sleepiness be something else? Like sleep apnea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Psychiatry suggested an outpatient sleep study to check for that. We’ll include that in your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I just want to feel more alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also check your blood counts. Your labs show low white blood cells, hemoglobin, and platelets—this is called pancytopenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had low counts before. Is this worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s worse. We’ll monitor it closely. We may need a bone marrow biopsy to see why your counts are low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Is it necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important to rule out any relapse or marrow issue. It’s a quick procedure with local numbing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it if it helps figure things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We also noticed your kidney function is a bit off—creatinine is 1.5, up from your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild. We’ll give IV fluids and monitor it. It may be due to dehydration or meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking much lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain it. We’ll help you rehydrate. Your CT chest showed improvement from your past MRSA pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I still cough a little, but it’s better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, occasional cough is expected. Your CT head showed no new bleeding or tumor—your old surgical area is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back with no growth—no infection found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the fever yesterday wasn’t from an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly not. You had a low-grade fever of 100.4 with low white blood cells. We started antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t take the vancomycin. I was worried about my kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Since you’re not spiking fevers and cultures are clean, we’ll stop the cefepime today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any update on my blood counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re still low. We’ll give a dose of Neupogen to help your white count and schedule the bone marrow biopsy for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my kidney numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Creatinine improved to 1.1 with fluids. It’s now 1.3—still a bit high, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI brain came back—no new lesions or signs of lymphoma. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge relief. So what’s causing the sleepiness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely your medications. You’re on several that cause drowsiness—methadone, pregabalin, clonazepam, dronabinol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what should I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend discussing with your provider about reducing or spacing them out. For now, we’re cutting duloxetine to once daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for anxiety and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep clonazepam available for anxiety, but use it only when needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bone marrow biopsy was done this morning. It’ll take a few days for results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It went well. Your counts improved a bit after Neupogen—WBC is now 3.0, but still low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re decreasing sirolimus to 0.5 mg daily and stopping pantoprazole and ursodiol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why stop those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pantoprazole can affect blood counts, and ursodiol isn’t needed now that you’re past day 100 post-transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. Your mental status is clear, and your gait is steady with your cane.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch for more falls, excessive sleepiness, fever, or bleeding. Your CBC needs to be checked soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bone marrow results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your oncologist. They’ll get the results and decide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I still do the sleep study?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a good idea to rule out sleep apnea. We’ll send the referral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take duloxetine once daily, sirolimus 0.5 mg in the morning, and the rest as listed. Avoid unnecessary sedatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll review them with my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going home with services. Your mom will help, and you have a walker if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and a lot of ostomy output. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain started a few days ago—sharp and crampy, mostly on the right side. And my ostomy bag has been filling up so fast, I’m changing it 8 to 10 times a day. It’s green and watery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea, yes, but no vomiting. I haven’t been eating much—just sipping fluids. And I had a fever at home, about 102, but Tylenol and Dilaudid helped a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from the ER. It shows thickening in part of your small intestine near the surgical connection. That could explain the pain and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it an infection? Or could it be the lymphoma coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. Right now, we’re thinking it’s likely enteritis—probably viral. We’ve ruled out C. diff and other bacterial infections. Your lymphoma is still in remission based on your last PET scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s a relief. But why so much fluid loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The inflamed bowel isn’t absorbing fluids properly. That’s why you’re losing so much. We’ve started IV fluids and will keep monitoring your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling weak. Is that from the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your labs show low potassium, which can make you feel tired and weak. We’re giving you potassium through the IV and will send more blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about my transplant? Is this GVHD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering that. But GVHD usually causes bloody diarrhea and weight loss over time. Your symptoms came on quickly, and your stool tests are negative for blood and infection markers. It’s less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my other meds? I’m on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your essential ones—methadone for pain, tacrolimus for transplant, and your asthma and thyroid meds. We held metformin since you’re not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics I got in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing cipro and flagyl for now, just in case there’s a bacterial cause. But if all tests stay negative, we’ll stop them and let your body clear the virus on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures and CMV test came back negative. No sign of those infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the stool tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also negative—for C. diff, salmonella, parasites, everything. The viral culture is still pending, but it’s looking more like viral enteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I just need to ride it out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pretty much. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids and electrolytes. Your fever’s gone down, and your pain is better with Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad the fever’s gone. I was worried it meant something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good sign. We’ll keep watching your labs. Your platelets and white count are low, but they’ve been that way since your transplant, so we’re not too concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ostomy output has decreased—from over a liter a day to about 500 mL. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I only changed my bag three times last night. That’s much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to stop the IV antibiotics today since all tests are negative. You’ll go home on a short course of oral cipro and metronidazole just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still a bit low. We’ll send you home with potassium pills for three days. Make sure to take them with food to avoid stomach upset.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more blood transfusions? My hemoglobin was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is 8.0 now, which is low but stable. Since you’re not bleeding and feeling okay, we won’t transfuse. It should improve as you eat more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my tacrolimus level? I remember last time it was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked it this morning. It’s <2.0, which is low. But since you’re on sirolimus now too, we’ll let your transplant team adjust it at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ll follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stool viral culture came back negative—no virus found. That supports our diagnosis of self-limited enteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was probably just a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. Your body fought it off. You’re eating again, your output is near normal, and you’re not febrile. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you develop fever, severe pain, or if your ostomy output increases again. Keep taking the antibiotics and potassium as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have appointments with your transplant team and oncologist. They’ll monitor your counts and overall status. Also, keep taking your budesonide—it helps with bowel inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re finalizing your discharge. Your vitals are stable, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discharge you around noon. You’ll take home prescriptions for the antibiotics, potassium, and your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin? I see it on the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a precaution. It’s oral vancomycin, which stays in the gut. It’s to prevent any C. diff, especially since you’ve been on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And sirolimus—why was that added?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your transplant team started it to help with immune regulation. It works with tacrolimus. Take it at 6 a.m. as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that. Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep up with your IVIG every four weeks. It’s important for your immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have it scheduled. I won’t miss it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be in touch. Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. You were admitted because of fever and worsening diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had more frequent and watery output from my stoma, and I’ve felt weak. I had a low-grade fever at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve had a stem cell transplant recently and have a colostomy. We’re concerned this could be graft-versus-host disease, or GVHD, affecting your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: GVHD again? I thought that was under control. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen after transplant. We’re taking it seriously. We’ll start you on IV steroids to calm the inflammation. We also need to rule out infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be on IV fluids too? I feel dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve already started IV fluids. We’re also checking your labs and will do a CT scan to look at your intestines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures and stool tests didn’t show any bacterial or viral infections. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? What is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s GVHD. A biopsy confirmed inflammation in your gut from your donor immune cells attacking your tissues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So the steroids will help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve started IV methylprednisolone at 50 mg daily. We’ll monitor your response and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CMV test back. Your viral load is low but detectable. This is common with immunosuppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: CMV? I’ve had that before. Do I need treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting ganciclovir to prevent it from worsening. It’s given every 12 hours through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me feel worse? I’m already so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause fatigue, but we’ll monitor your blood counts closely. The benefit outweighs the risk right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting TPN today because you’re not absorbing enough nutrition through your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: TPN? Is that like IV nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it delivers nutrients directly into your bloodstream. It helps your gut rest and heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV viral load improved—from 370 to 190. That’s a good sign the ganciclovir is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can stop the IV medicine soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll keep it going and recheck in a few days. We want to make sure it drops further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stoma looks a bit inflamed. We’re adding metronidazole just in case there’s a bacterial component.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. It might be related to GVHD or irritation. We’ll watch it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a CT scan today for new abdominal pain. Good news—no appendicitis or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But there was something on the scan, right? You looked concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw some new lung opacities. We’re following up with a chest CT to check for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest CT shows patchy opacities in your lower lungs. It looks like pneumonia, likely from a virus or mild infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? But I’m not coughing much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some patients don’t have classic symptoms, especially with weakened immunity. We’re starting cefepime and azithromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. Your oxygen levels are good. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool output has improved—from 650 cc to 300 cc daily—and it’s thicker. That means your gut is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re advancing you to Phase V of the GI GVHD diet—soft, low-residue foods. We’ll go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you IV immunoglobulin today. Your IgG levels were low, so this helps boost your immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to get that every few weeks. I’ve missed a few doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll resume regular IVIG after discharge. It’s important for preventing infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV viral load is now undetectable. We’ll switch you to oral valganciclovir before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can stop the IV medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll transition to a once-daily pill. You’ll take it at home for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture showed some staph, but it’s not resistant. It’s likely just colonizing, not causing infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be on antibiotics for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we don’t think it’s causing harm. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes were a bit high, but they’re improving. Likely due to medications, not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which meds are affecting my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tacrolimus and voriconazole can. We’re watching levels and adjusting doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off TPN for two days and eating well. That’s a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually hungry! That feels good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. We’ll keep you on the soft diet and monitor your stoma output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg swelling was checked with an ultrasound. No blood clot—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that. What’s causing the swelling then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely fluid overload from IV fluids and TPN. It should improve now that we’ve stopped them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
